Maryland Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession: What Owners Should Know

Cash Home Buyers in Maryland

Selling a Maryland House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is. Tell us about the property and the timeline.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Maryland statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we do not state it.

Maryland law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Within 20 years from the date the cause of action accrues, a person must file an action for recovery of possession of a corporeal freehold or leasehold estate in land. (Md. Code, Courts & Judicial Proceedings § 5-103(a)(1); source)
  • Before an eviction, the landlord must get a judgment in a rent court / breach of lease / holding over case and then petition for a Warrant of Restitution; the sheriff or constable must be present at the eviction, and it cannot occur on a Sunday or holiday. (Housing Cases (Maryland Courts); source)
Selling in Maryland?
We buy Maryland houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Details we could not confirm on an official page are not stated here. Read the statute sections linked above for the full text, and confirm deadlines with the court or county office.

How to sell a Maryland house when this applies to you

  1. Write down who is in the house and on what terms: owner, heirs, tenants or occupants with no lease.
  2. Ask the title company what it needs to insure the sale, such as a recorded deed, court papers or a payoff letter.
  3. Get the payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the proceeds at closing.
  4. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. See we buy houses in Maryland.

What a cash sale of a Maryland house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Maryland.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Maryland disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Maryland

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Maryland change, so confirm details with the official office or a Maryland attorney or tax professional.

More questions about selling in Maryland

How fast can I close on a cash sale?

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

Do I have to clean out or repair the house?

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

Is there any cost to request an offer?

No. Requesting an offer is free and carries no obligation.

Maryland Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Maryland house?

Only by meeting every requirement of the adverse possession statute cited above for the full period. Check the statute and talk to a Maryland attorney about your facts.

Can I sell a house that has squatters in it?

Yes. We buy houses as-is, including occupied ones. Tell us who is in the property when you request an offer.

Should I remove a squatter myself?

No. Use the legal process described in the official sources above. Self-help removal can create liability for the owner.

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Maryland statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we do not state it.

Maryland statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • A landlord may not impose a security deposit in excess of the equivalent of 1 month's rent per dwelling unit, regardless of the number of tenants; a landlord who overcharges is liable for up to three times the extra amount plus attorney's fees. (Md. Code, Real Property § 8-203(b)(1), (b)(3); source)
  • Within 45 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit with simple interest (greater of the daily U.S. Treasury yield curve rate for 1 year or 1.5% a year), less damages rightfully withheld. (Real Property § 8-203(e)(1); source)
  • If any deposit is withheld, the landlord must mail an itemized list of damages and costs within 45 days after the tenancy ends or forfeits the right to withhold for damages; wrongful failure to return can cost up to threefold plus attorney's fees. (Real Property § 8-203(e)(4), (g); source)
  • For a written lease for a term over 1 week or a month-to-month tenancy, notice to terminate is 60 days before expiration of the tenancy; year-to-year is 90 days; week-to-week is 7 days (written lease) or 21 days (no written lease). (Real Property § 8-402(b)-(c); source)
  • A tenant may use rent escrow (paying rent to a third party/court) where the landlord fails to fix defects after notice; the tenant must first notify the landlord of defects and request repairs. (Housing Cases (Maryland Courts); source)

Cash Offer in 24 Hours

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Maryland statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we do not state it.

Maryland law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Before filing a failure-to-pay-rent case, landlord must give the tenant written notice of intent to file, giving 10 days to cure, on a Judiciary-created form (DC-CV-115); the complaint must state the date notice was given. (Real Property § 8-401(c); source)
  • Nonpayment cases are filed in the District Court; the judgment orders possession within 4 days after trial (extendable up to 15 days with a physician certificate); if the tenant tenders rent, late fees and costs at trial, the complaint is satisfied. (Real Property § 8-401; source)
  • If the tenant does not comply within 7 days of a landlord judgment, the court issues a warrant of restitution to a county official, who may remove the tenant's goods. (Real Property § 8-401(f)(1); source)
  • Breach of lease: landlord must give 30 days' written notice that the tenant is in violation and the landlord wants to repossess (one of the alternatives in the section). (Real Property § 8-402.1; source)
  • No-cause/end of term: 60 days' notice for month-to-month tenancy or a written term lease over 1 week; 90 days for year-to-year. (Real Property § 8-402; source)
  • Landlord must notify tenant of the eviction date at least 6 days before eviction (mail with certificate of mailing, post on property, and send electronically if email/cell known); the sheriff or constable carries out the eviction. (Housing Cases (Maryland Courts); Real Property § 8-407; source)
